analysis.one_liner: Strips the labor board of its power to enforce workers' rights against employers.
analysis.headline: A bill to remove the National Labor Relations Board's power to enforce labor law died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so the National Labor Relations Board could only investigate claims of unfair labor practices — not issue complaints, prosecute them, make rules affecting workers' or employers' rights, or ask courts to enforce its orders. Instead, individual workers would have to sue their employers in federal court on their own. The board would essentially become an office that takes notes and files reports.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers accused of firing workers for union activity or other unfair labor practices. Today, the board's general counsel investigates charges and prosecutes them before the board, and the board can seek court enforcement at no cost to the worker. Under this bill, the employer would face no board prosecution and a worker would have to hire a lawyer and sue in federal court — a far higher barrier. Employers would also gain from the ban on board rulemaking, which would freeze labor protections as written decades ago.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the board general counsel's authority to issue and prosecute unfair labor practice complaints, leaving only investigation of allegations [S2][S3].

Limits board rulemaking to its internal functions and prohibits any regulations affecting the substantive or procedural rights of employers, employees, or unions, including rules on unfair labor practices and representation elections [S2][S3].

Repeals the board's authority to prevent unfair labor practices and its power to petition courts for enforcement of orders or seek injunctions, replacing board prosecution with private civil actions brought by the aggrieved person [S2][S3].
Requires the board, within six months of enactment, to revise or rescind existing regulations to conform to the new limits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who rely on the labor board — especially lower-wage employees who cannot afford a federal lawsuit — would lose free enforcement of their rights to organize, bargain, and be protected from retaliation. Unions would lose a board that can certify elections, make rules, and enforce orders.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers seeking to organize or bargain

drawbacks.text: Workers would bear the full cost of enforcement: the bill replaces board prosecution with private civil actions in federal court, which require hiring a lawyer and can take years — a barrier most individual employees cannot afford [S2][S3].

The bill's limits on rulemaking would prevent the board from updating election procedures and unfair labor practice standards, locking in workplace protections as they stood when the law was written, even as workplaces change [S2][S3].

Supporters would argue the board wields too much power over employers and that private lawsuits are a fairer check; the bill responds to complaints that board decisions and rules in recent years favored unions and burdened businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift the entire burden of enforcing federal labor law from a public agency onto individual workers, most of whom cannot litigate against their employer. Employers would gain a system where violating labor law carries little practical risk. Any benefit to employers from reduced board oversight comes directly at the expense of workers' ability to organize without retaliation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on July 20, 2017, with five Republican cosponsors: Sens. Cruz, Lankford, Cotton, Strange, and Rubio [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions keep the existing labor board enforcement system, since the bill died without a vote. Employers who would have benefited from weakened enforcement are no better off, but neither faced a floor vote on the record.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the National Labor Relations Board of its complaint, rulemaking, and enforcement powers.

for.name: 5 of 52 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Cruz, Lankford, Cotton, Strange, and Rubio).

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action after its referral and died at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, and the Republican-chaired committee never advanced it.

industries.note: The bill would make it far harder for the labor board to prosecute companies for firing or retaliating against workers, and would bar new board rules affecting employers' rights. The industry's gain — weaker enforcement — comes directly at workers' expense.

Unions rely on board complaint prosecution, rulemaking on election procedures, and court enforcement of board orders; the bill repeals all three. Their interest here runs alongside the rights of the workers they represent.
